Ductless trouble signs

What happens at the indoor head?

A ductless fault can affect one room or every head connected to the outdoor unit. Record the symptom, current mode, and any error display before booking. These cards outline possible causes and safe observations. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models; an on-site diagnosis determines the actual fault.

One head runs but the room stays warm Book soon

Likely causes

  • A clogged filter restricts the air leaving the head.
  • A refrigerant fault limits cooling even while the fan runs.
  • Furniture or a closed doorway blocks air from reaching the occupied space.

Check safely first

  • Check the mode and set temperature against the manual.
  • Keep curtains and furniture clear of the head.
  • Note whether other heads cool normally.

What the technician does

A technician can compare the affected head with the other zones, assess airflow, and test for a refrigerant or control fault.

Repair timing depends on the fault and any parts needed.

When to act: Book service if the room remains uncomfortable.

Water drips from the indoor head Book soon

Likely causes

  • Debris obstructs the condensate drain.
  • A drainage fault prevents water from leaving the head.
  • Ice melts and overflows after restricted airflow or another operating fault.

Check safely first

  • Switch the affected head off using its control.
  • Protect flooring and move belongings away from the drip.
  • Keep hands and tools out of the head.

What the technician does

A technician can trace the water path, inspect the drain route, and check whether icing caused the overflow. Clearing water alone may leave the cause unresolved.

Drain access and the cause determine the visit length.

When to act: Stop the affected head while water is leaking indoors.

The head will not respond to the remote Book soon

Likely causes

  • The remote batteries are depleted or installed incorrectly.
  • A timer or mode setting prevents the expected response.
  • A receiver, power, or communication fault prevents the head from operating.

Check safely first

  • Check the batteries and settings in the operating manual.
  • Point the remote toward the head without a curtain blocking it.
  • Photograph any displayed code or blinking light.
  • Avoid repeated resets that erase the fault history.

What the technician does

A technician can distinguish a remote problem from a head control fault and test communication with the outdoor equipment before recommending parts.

Some control faults need a model-specific replacement part.

When to act: Arrange service if basic control checks do not restore operation.

Several heads stop at the same time Book soon

Likely causes

  • A shared outdoor unit fault interrupts every connected zone.
  • A common power or communication problem prevents normal operation.
  • Incompatible heating and cooling requests put some multi-zone systems into standby.

Check safely first

  • Record the operating mode shown for each head.
  • Note which heads stopped and whether a code appeared.
  • Leave electrical covers closed.

What the technician does

A technician can compare zone requests and inspect the shared equipment. The fault may sit outside the room where the loss of comfort was first noticed.

Shared equipment testing may require access outside the home.

When to act: Book service for a fault affecting all connected rooms.

Likely causes

  • Restricted airflow allows ice to form during cooling.
  • A refrigerant or control fault affects operation.

Check safely first

  • Switch the head off and protect finishes below it.
  • Do not chip ice or apply heat.

What the technician does

A technician can test airflow and operating conditions after the ice clears to identify the cause.

Ice may need to clear before full testing can proceed.

When to act: Turn the affected head off and arrange service.

Likely causes

  • Moisture and dirt remain inside the head.
  • A drainage fault leaves standing water.

Check safely first

  • Note whether the odor starts with fan or cooling mode.
  • Avoid spraying cleaners into the head.

What the technician does

A technician can inspect the head and drainage path to determine the cleaning or repair needed.

Cleaning scope depends on access and the source of the odor.

The head rattles or makes a new vibration Book soon

Likely causes

  • A loose cover or mounting point vibrates during operation.
  • A dirty or damaged fan creates unusual noise.
  • Vibration travels along refrigerant piping or through a wall.

Check safely first

  • Record the sound from a safe distance.
  • Note whether it changes with fan speed.
  • Keep hands away from moving parts and covers.
  • For smoke or sparking, leave the area and call emergency services.

What the technician does

A technician can locate the vibration source and distinguish a head fault from noise carried through the mounting or piping. The source may differ from the loudest spot.

Access to the mounting and piping can affect repair timing.

When to act: Stop operation for harsh grinding or a burning smell.

An attic zone struggles in heating mode Book soon

Likely causes

  • The selected equipment cannot meet the room load in current conditions.
  • An airflow or refrigerant fault reduces available heat.
  • A setting, sensor, or normal operating pause changes heat delivery.

Check safely first

  • Check the heating mode and temperature setting in the manual.
  • Record outdoor conditions and how long the loss of heat lasts.
  • Note whether other zones are heating normally.
  • Avoid opening equipment or repeatedly cycling the power.

What the technician does

A technician can distinguish a fault from an equipment capacity limit. A cold attic may also need its insulation and air leakage assessed before replacing working equipment.

Diagnosis should account for the weather when the problem occurs.

When to act: Book service if occupied rooms cannot stay warm.

The head stops and displays an error Book soon

Likely causes

  • A sensor reports a condition outside its expected range.
  • A communication fault interrupts coordination between connected equipment.
  • An operating fault triggers a protective shutdown.

Check safely first

  • Photograph the complete code or blinking sequence.
  • Record the mode and which heads were running.
  • Keep the model number available for the service call.
  • Do not use an unrelated model manual to interpret the code.

What the technician does

A technician can use the model-specific fault information and tests to identify the cause. An error display guides diagnosis; it does not prove one part has failed.

Parts availability and testing needs determine the repair schedule.

When to act: Arrange diagnosis rather than repeatedly clearing the code.

Rooms without ductwork

Ductless layouts for Chicago homes

Single-room ductless mini-split

An addition or enclosed room can have a dedicated comfort zone without extending ducts. The head needs a place that lets air reach the occupied space. Outdoor placement, piping, and drainage still need to work together. Plan one indoor head and an outdoor location with clear airflow and service access.

Ductless for several rooms

A multi-zone layout can serve several rooms through a shared outdoor unit and compatible indoor heads. The number of heads does not settle capacity or mode limits. A proposal should identify the complete combination and the rooms served. Where the selected system uses a branch box, its location must remain accessible for service.

Ductless for an attic

Roof exposure, insulation, and sloped ceilings shape an attic layout. A sloped ceiling can limit head placement; leave room above the head and a safe way to reach its filters.

Ductless for an addition

An addition can have a dedicated comfort zone without depending on air traveling through a doorway. Separate control lets an addition respond to its own sun exposure and room use.

Ductless for a condo

Condo planning brings the indoor location together with association rules, shared exterior space, and service access. An attractive wall location cannot settle those outside constraints. Agree on approvals and routes before work begins. Association approval should precede a wall penetration or any work affecting common property.

Ductless in a two-flat

A two-flat may have different comfort needs on each floor. Zone planning should follow room use and doors. Ownership and responsibility for service also matter. Per-floor zoning should keep shared outdoor equipment accessible for service.

Ductless HVAC questions

Can a ductless mini-split serve an addition without new ducts?

A ductless mini-split can serve an addition without extending the existing ductwork. The room still needs a suitable indoor head location, an outdoor unit location, and a route for refrigerant lines and drainage. City & Suburban offers ductless installation and repairs all makes and models.

Does one indoor head cool several closed bedrooms?

A single-zone system pairs one head with one outdoor unit. One head cannot give several closed bedrooms separate control: walls and closed doors limit airflow. A multi-zone system uses compatible heads sharing an outdoor unit, but mode limits still depend on the model. A bedroom used with the door shut may need its own head.

Can a ductless system provide both heating and cooling?

A ductless system designed for heating and cooling can provide both from the same equipment. Winter suitability depends on the selected model and its heating output at cold outdoor temperatures. An attic or addition needs a winter comfort plan, including whether another heat source must remain available.

What should a condo owner settle before ductless installation?

Condo planning should settle association approval, outdoor equipment placement, wall penetrations, drainage, and access for future service. Shared walls and roof space may limit the route even when the room has a clear place for a head. Written approval should precede work that affects common property.

What can a homeowner check when a ductless remote does nothing?

Check the remote batteries, displayed mode, and timer settings against the operating manual. Note any light pattern on the head before changing settings. A visible display does not prove the indoor and outdoor equipment are communicating. City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows.

What information helps with booking a ductless repair?

Provide the indoor and outdoor model numbers, affected rooms, current mode, and any error display. Note whether all heads stopped together or only one room lost comfort. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models. Photos taken safely from floor level can help describe a leak or the location of the equipment.

Is there a maintenance plan for a home with ductless equipment?

City & Suburban offers maintenance plans with seasonal check-ups, priority dispatch, and member discounts. Before enrolling, confirm how the plan applies to the ductless equipment and how many heads are included. A home with several zones should identify each indoor head and the shared outdoor unit at booking.

Which ductless brands does City & Suburban install and service?

City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment and repairs all makes and models. An existing mini-split from another manufacturer can still be serviced. Provide the indoor and outdoor model numbers at booking so the service request identifies the equipment and connected heads.

What backs a ductless installation?

City & Suburban gives an upfront written price before work, with no hidden fees. Equipment warranty terms come from the manufacturer and should be confirmed in writing with the quote. The written terms should identify coverage, registration requirements, and any exclusions, including how labor and future service are handled.

Does a ductless system cost less to run?

Variable-speed ductless equipment can use less electricity than single-speed window units or resistance heat by adjusting output to the room load. Savings depend on the selected model, weather, insulation, settings, and the equipment replaced. Compare expected use for the actual rooms; lower running costs are not guaranteed.

Ductless mini-splits answer a problem that is ordinary in Chicago: a room, a floor or a whole condo with no ductwork to carry conditioned air. A greystone attic. A coach house. A rear addition off a steam-heated two-flat. This guide covers how a mini-split works, which buildings suit one, how single-zone and multi-zone systems differ, where heads and line sets belong in masonry walls, what usually fails, what maintenance keeps a system honest, and what a correct installation day looks like. City & Suburban has worked on Chicago systems since 1952.

Key takeaways

  • A ductless mini-split moves heat through a copper refrigerant line instead of ducts, so one outdoor unit can cool a room in July and heat it in January.
  • Cook County Assessor records count 306,261 of 439,398 residential properties in the eight Chicago townships with no central cooling, which is why ductless work is common here.
  • Zone count matters more than head size: one oversized head in a hallway conditions the hallway, while a multi-zone system gives each room its own control.
  • Most ductless service calls trace back to airflow or water, not refrigerant: a fouled blower wheel, a blocked drain line or a dirty outdoor coil.
  • Installing new equipment generally needs a City of Chicago permit; whether other work needs one is worth confirming with the City.

What is a ductless mini-split, and how does it heat and cool without ducts?

SHORT ANSWER

A ductless mini-split is two pieces: an outdoor compressor unit and one or more indoor heads, joined by a copper refrigerant line set instead of ductwork. The system moves heat in either direction, so the same equipment cools in summer and heats in the colder months. City & Suburban installs and repairs ductless systems in Chicago homes where no ducts exist, or where adding them would mean losing ceiling height.

Picture a rehabbed attic in a Logan Square two-flat. The space gets steam heat from the building below and a window unit wedged into a dormer. In July the room runs eight degrees warmer than the floor beneath it. In March the heat arrives whether the room needs it or not. No duct reaches the third floor, and adding one would cut into the only closet. This is the room a mini-split was built for, and the one case where cooling services and heating arrive in the same cabinet.

The usual fix is a stack of appliances. A window unit for summer, a space heater for winter, a box fan to push air down the stairs. The cost lands in three places. The window is blocked from May to October, and the noise sits in the room. The electric bill climbs too, because resistance heat uses more electricity than a heat pump for the same warmth and a single-speed window unit cycles at full output. Some of these appliances have thermostats, but each serves only the spot where it sits.

What changed is the compressor. An inverter-driven compressor varies its speed instead of cycling on and off, so a mini-split can hold a room within a degree at part load. The line set, usually two insulated copper tubes and a control cable, replaces the duct entirely. A reversing valve sends heat the other way in winter, pulling warmth out of cold outdoor air. One cabinet outside, both seasons, controlled room by room.

A ductless quote starts as a room question before an equipment question. Which rooms are uncomfortable, what the walls are made of, where an outdoor unit can sit, how far the line set has to run. City & Suburban sends NATE-certified technicians, diagnoses before anything is quoted, and prices upfront with no hidden fees. Installed equipment is American Standard, and City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, so a mini-split left behind by another installer is still serviceable.

The scale of the problem sits in the public record. Cook County Assessor data for the eight townships covering Chicago counts 439,398 residential properties, and 306,261 of those have no central cooling. That count covers houses and small multi-family buildings, not large apartment buildings. Ductless is not a niche product in this city. For much of the housing stock it is the only route to cooling that does not start with new ductwork.

Which Chicago buildings end up with no ductwork, and where does a mini-split fit?

SHORT ANSWER

Much of Chicago's older housing stock heats with steam or hot water and may have no usable air ducts. Additions, attics and coach houses were finished long after the mechanical layout was set. City & Suburban installs ductless systems in exactly those spaces: third-floor conversions, garden units, sunrooms and rooms over a garage. Condos where a shaft wall blocks every duct route are the other common case.

Four building types come up again and again. The pre-1940 greystone or two-flat with steam and hot-water heat and often no usable duct in the building. The bungalow with a finished attic above a single trunk line. The condo carved out of a courtyard building, where the only wall facing outside is the one with the windows. And the rear addition, built decades later onto a house whose mechanical room is forty feet away.

The default answer is to extend the ducts. In a masonry building that means a soffit down a hallway, a chase cut through a closet, or joists drilled where drilling becomes a structural question. The homeowner pays twice: once for carpentry and patching that adds no comfort, and again in lost space. In a condo, the board has to approve the work before any of it starts.

A single-zone mini-split often needs only a small sleeve through one wall, sized to the manufacturer's line set and drain requirements. Multiple heads, fire-rated walls and condensate routes can need more penetrations or more work. Where the line set, control cable and drain share one hole, it is pitched down to shed water. This changes which rooms are candidates. A finished attic, a garden-level office or a four-season room can be conditioned without touching the rest of the building. The existing system is not asked to carry a load it was not sized for.

The building decides the system here, because the wall, the drain path and the outdoor location set the limits of what can be installed. Where ducts already exist and are in reasonable shape, an AC installation is the other route, and City & Suburban quotes that work too. City & Suburban is family-owned, has worked in Chicago since 1952, and serves 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs, so these building types are familiar ones.

Cook County Assessor records put 98,849 of those residential properties on hot water or steam heat, so many of these buildings may lack usable air distribution; an inspection confirms what is actually there. In West Chicago township, covering Wicker Park and West Town, 83.0% of properties date from before 1940. Ductwork was never part of the original plan across much of this city, and retrofitting it is a construction project rather than a mechanical one.

  • Coach house or room over a garage with no mechanical room of its own
  • Rear addition or four-season room built long after the original layout
  • Garden unit or basement office that runs cold in winter and damp in summer
  • Condo in a courtyard building heated by the building, with no chase for a duct

Single-zone or multi-zone: how many ductless heads does a home need?

SHORT ANSWER

One head conditions one open space. It does not push air around a corner or up a stairwell. A single-zone system suits one room or a small open floor. A multi-zone system runs several heads off one outdoor unit, each with its own control; how many depends on the model, its minimum modulation and its shared-mode limits. City & Suburban prices ductless work upfront with no hidden fees, so the cost of a second or third zone is clear before the job starts.

The first request is almost always for one large head to handle a whole floor. In a 1920s Chicago layout with a center hallway and doors on both sides, that does not work. Conditioned air follows the shortest return path, so the hallway reaches the setting, the head satisfies and shuts down, and the two bedrooms stay as warm as before. Open-plan rehabs are the exception, not the rule.

The common response is to oversize. A head rated well above the room's load feels safer, and one zone is a cheaper quote than three. The cost arrives later. An oversized head reaches the setting fast, drops to its minimum output, and stops pulling humidity out of the air, so the room feels clammy at 72 degrees. Short cycling also wears the parts that cycle.

The mechanism most quotes skip is minimum capacity. A multi-zone outdoor unit has a floor below which it cannot modulate, and every head draws from that same compressor. Three small heads on a large outdoor unit can leave the system running above the load of any single room. Matching each head to its room, and the sum of the heads to the outdoor unit, is the real design work. The same modulation limits show up in any heat pump service call on a ducted system.

Zone layout is the decision that comes before equipment selection on this kind of job. A two-zone system with correctly matched heads usually holds temperature better than a three-zone system built around one oversized head. Pro tip: Count the doors. Any room that closes off from the head's airflow needs its own zone, a transfer path, or a different plan.

Where do ductless heads, line sets and drains belong in an older building?

SHORT ANSWER

Head placement decides comfort, noise and how the installation looks for the next decade. A wall head wants clear throw across the room, a return path back to its underside, and several inches of clearance above it. Head location, sleeve position and drain route are settled before any hole is drilled, because moving a head later means patching brick. City & Suburban installs and repairs ductless systems across 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs.

Chicago walls complicate this. Exterior walls are often solid masonry three bricks thick, and interior walls may be plaster over lath. A 1920s layout rarely offers a chase from the third floor down to grade. Add a bay window, a fire escape and a lot line four feet away, and the number of workable routes drops fast. The best wall for comfort and the easiest wall to drill are seldom the same wall.

Many installs follow the easiest path for the crew. The head goes on the wall nearest the outdoor unit. The line set runs down the front of the building in a white cover, and the drain ties into whatever is close. The homeowner lives with the result. Air blows straight into a ceiling fan, a cover crosses the front facade, and a drain backs up into the head two summers later.

Three details decide whether that happens. Throw: a wall head should blow along the long axis of the room, not into a wall six feet away. Fall: a gravity drain needs roughly a quarter inch of drop per foot, or else a condensate pump with a safety switch. Length and lift: every line set has a maximum run and a maximum height difference, and both change the refrigerant charge the system needs.

Good practice on an older building is to agree head locations, sleeve position and drain fall before drilling. The line set then runs on the least visible elevation the building allows. Mounting hardware belongs in masonry rather than trim, and the sleeve is sealed and pitched so rain drains outward. City & Suburban works in 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs, listed on the service areas page.

Drain trouble is not theoretical in Chicago condos. Larry V. (Jul 2025) called about "water leaks related to a clogged condensation pipe above my condo unit". The outdoor equipment got a look on the same trip. Any indoor coil that makes water needs somewhere for that water to go, by gravity or by pump. A head mounted without that plan sends the water down the wall.

Pro tip: Before the hole is drilled, stand where the furniture goes and look at the wall. A head six inches off center is a fifteen-year annoyance.

How does a ductless system handle heat in a Chicago winter?

SHORT ANSWER

A ductless head heats by reversing the refrigerant cycle, and in one room it often becomes the main heat source for that space. Capacity falls as the outdoor temperature drops, and the system pauses to defrost its outdoor coil. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment. Whether the building's existing heat stays in place as backup depends on the model's cold-weather output, the room's heat loss and the building's requirements, so confirm the winter plan in the quote.

Chicago asks more of a heating system than a cooling one. A rehabbed attic that needs a window unit for ten weeks may need heat for six months. In a condo where the building supplies heat, the code baseline is a floor rather than a comfort setting. A top-floor room facing north often sits below it on a windy February night.

The usual plan treats ductless as a summer purchase and ignores the heating half. The head gets sized for the cooling load, which in Chicago is the smaller of the two loads. Then December arrives and the zone cannot hold temperature on a design-day morning. The electric space heater comes back out, which is the most expensive heat in the building.

Two mechanisms explain that. Output drops as the outdoor temperature falls, because there is less heat in the outdoor air to move. A head rated for a room in cooling can therefore be short in heating. The outdoor coil also frosts, so the system reverses for several minutes to melt it and the head stops blowing warm air. Neither behavior is a fault. Both need planning around.

On a room where ductless carries the winter, the heating load sets the head size, not the cooling load. Whether to keep the existing heat as backup depends on cold-weather output, room heat loss and building requirements, and the winter plan belongs in the written quote. For whole-house questions, heat pump services answer a different problem than a single-zone mini-split. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment, diagnoses before quoting, and prices upfront with no hidden fees.

The legal baseline is worth knowing. Under the Chicago Heat Ordinance (Municipal Code 13-196-410), heat supplied by a landlord has a floor from September 15 to June 1. The requirement is at least 68 degrees from 8:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m., and 66 degrees overnight. The code lists exceptions, so it stands as the general rule. A ductless zone is often what closes the gap between that floor and comfort.

Pro tip: Where ductless is the only heat in a room, the heating load sets the head size. Sizing for the cooling load alone is a common reason a ductless zone disappoints in January.

What usually goes wrong with a ductless mini-split, and what fixes it?

SHORT ANSWER

Most ductless service calls come down to airflow or water rather than refrigerant. The usual causes are a fouled blower wheel, a blocked drain, a dirty outdoor coil, or a communication fault between head and outdoor unit. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, diagnoses before anything is quoted, and offers same-day service when the schedule allows.

Two complaints dominate ductless calls. A head that runs but no longer cools, and a head that drips down the wall in July. Both tend to show up in the third or fourth summer. Both get lived with for a few weeks first, because a mini-split failing slowly is easy to ignore.

The common assumption is low refrigerant. A sealed system does not consume refrigerant, so a system that is low has a leak, and adding more without finding the leak buys one season. The other default move is a filter rinse. Rinsing the two mesh filters takes five minutes and helps, but it does not reach the part that actually fouls.

That part is the blower wheel. A ductless head pulls room air across a small barrel fan and a cold coil, and over years a film builds on the blades and the coil fins. Airflow falls, the coil runs colder, condensate misses the pan, and water finds the wall. The same film is what makes a head smell on startup. A ducted system fails differently, which is why an AC repair call follows another sequence.

City & Suburban diagnoses before anything is quoted. The readings that matter on a ductless call are airflow at the head, the temperature split across the coil, drain flow and pressures at the service port. A fouled blower wheel and coil are a cleaning job before a replacement job. NATE-certified technicians do the work, and City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, including equipment it did not install.

The record on that approach is public. City & Suburban averages 4.98 across 204 Google reviews and holds an A+ rating with the BBB. Rob is named in review after review for explaining what was wrong before doing the work. A repair diagnosed once costs less than the same repair guessed at twice.

  • Water dripping from the head: blocked drain line, failed condensate pump, or a drain run with no fall
  • Musty smell at startup: film on the blower wheel and coil that a filter rinse cannot reach
  • One zone of a multi-zone system quits: control-cable or communication fault, or a branch box valve
  • Outdoor unit icing beyond a normal defrost: low charge, blocked coil, or a failed defrost sensor

A rattle or scrape inside the headDebris against the blower wheel, or a loose front panel
Gurgling or trickling at the wallRefrigerant running low, or condensate standing in the drain line

What maintenance does a ductless system need, and how long should it last?

SHORT ANSWER

A ductless system hides nothing in a duct, so everything that fouls is reachable: two mesh filters, the blower wheel, the indoor coil, the drain and the outdoor coil. Filters get rinsed monthly in season by the homeowner, and the rest is annual work. City & Suburban offers maintenance plans with seasonal check-ups, priority dispatch and member discounts.

A mini-split is quiet, and that is the problem. A system that fouls slowly never announces it, so the first sign is a drip, or a summer where the room never gets below 76 degrees. Meanwhile the equipment sits in the room, pulling the room's dust through itself all season. Typical service life for this equipment is 15 to 20 years, and a neglected head rarely gets there.

Most ductless systems in Chicago get no service at all. Nothing sits in a basement to walk past, and no filter rack reminds anyone. The monthly filter rinse in the manual rarely becomes a habit. The cost shows up as a compressor working against a dirty coil for years, and as a cleaning bill that a yearly visit would have avoided.

The useful shift is to split the work in two. Two mesh filters are a homeowner job, roughly monthly while the system runs. The blower wheel, the indoor coil, the drain and the outdoor coil are a technician job once a year. On a ductless head that often means pulling the cover and bagging the head for a wash, a step an AC maintenance visit on a ducted system never involves.

A thorough annual visit on a ductless system covers refrigerant pressures, drain flow, electrical connections and coil condition. Readings written down beat tasks ticked off, because capacity loss then shows up as a number rather than a complaint.

What happens on a ductless installation day, and what does the City require?

SHORT ANSWER

A single-zone ductless installation is usually a one-day job: bracket, sleeve, head, line set, outdoor unit, pressure test, vacuum, charge and commissioning. Multi-zone jobs run longer. Commissioning is the step that decides how the system performs in year four. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment and quotes upfront with no hidden fees.

Installation day in an occupied Chicago condo is a logistics problem as much as a mechanical one. Elevator reservations, a route for a ladder, a neighbor's parking space, and a lot line that leaves four feet for an outdoor unit. On a flat-roof building the equipment goes up the stairs. None of that changes the mechanical work, but it changes the schedule.

The fast version of this job skips the part nobody sees. The line set gets connected, the valves opened, and the system started within the hour. Skipping the nitrogen pressure test and the vacuum leaves air and moisture inside a sealed system, and moisture plus refrigerant oil makes acid. That failure arrives in year four, long after the crew has gone.

Commissioning is what separates one install from another. A nitrogen pressure test holds the joints under pressure before any refrigerant enters. A deep vacuum pulls the system down to a few hundred microns and then holds, proving it is dry and tight. Flare joints get torqued to spec rather than guessed, because a flare is the most common leak point on a ductless system.

Pressure test, vacuum and recorded commissioning readings are the standard a ductless quote should be measured against. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment, prices upfront with no hidden fees, and offers financing through Wells Fargo Home Projects subject to credit approval. Ductless trouble signs

What happens at the indoor head?

A ductless fault can affect one room or every head connected to the outdoor unit. Record the symptom, current mode, and any error display before booking. These cards outline possible causes and safe observations. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models; an on-site diagnosis determines the actual fault.

One head runs but the room stays warm Book soon

Likely causes

  • A clogged filter restricts the air leaving the head.
  • A refrigerant fault limits cooling even while the fan runs.
  • Furniture or a closed doorway blocks air from reaching the occupied space.

Check safely first

  • Check the mode and set temperature against the manual.
  • Keep curtains and furniture clear of the head.
  • Note whether other heads cool normally.

What the technician does

A technician can compare the affected head with the other zones, assess airflow, and test for a refrigerant or control fault.

Repair timing depends on the fault and any parts needed.

When to act: Book service if the room remains uncomfortable.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Water drips from the indoor head Book soon

Likely causes

  • Debris obstructs the condensate drain.
  • A drainage fault prevents water from leaving the head.
  • Ice melts and overflows after restricted airflow or another operating fault.

Check safely first

  • Switch the affected head off using its control.
  • Protect flooring and move belongings away from the drip.
  • Keep hands and tools out of the head.

What the technician does

A technician can trace the water path, inspect the drain route, and check whether icing caused the overflow. Clearing water alone may leave the cause unresolved.

Drain access and the cause determine the visit length.

When to act: Stop the affected head while water is leaking indoors.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
The head will not respond to the remote Book soon

Likely causes

  • The remote batteries are depleted or installed incorrectly.
  • A timer or mode setting prevents the expected response.
  • A receiver, power, or communication fault prevents the head from operating.

Check safely first

  • Check the batteries and settings in the operating manual.
  • Point the remote toward the head without a curtain blocking it.
  • Photograph any displayed code or blinking light.
  • Avoid repeated resets that erase the fault history.

What the technician does

A technician can distinguish a remote problem from a head control fault and test communication with the outdoor equipment before recommending parts.

Some control faults need a model-specific replacement part.

When to act: Arrange service if basic control checks do not restore operation.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Several heads stop at the same time Book soon

Likely causes

  • A shared outdoor unit fault interrupts every connected zone.
  • A common power or communication problem prevents normal operation.
  • Incompatible heating and cooling requests put some multi-zone systems into standby.

Check safely first

  • Record the operating mode shown for each head.
  • Note which heads stopped and whether a code appeared.
  • Leave electrical covers closed.

What the technician does

A technician can compare zone requests and inspect the shared equipment. The fault may sit outside the room where the loss of comfort was first noticed.

Shared equipment testing may require access outside the home.

When to act: Book service for a fault affecting all connected rooms.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
Ice appears on an indoor head Book soon

Likely causes

  • Restricted airflow allows ice to form during cooling.
  • A refrigerant or control fault affects operation.

Check safely first

  • Switch the head off and protect finishes below it.
  • Do not chip ice or apply heat.

What the technician does

A technician can test airflow and operating conditions after the ice clears to identify the cause.

Ice may need to clear before full testing can proceed.

When to act: Turn the affected head off and arrange service.

Book a visit Call (773) 238-3838
A sour or musty smell comes from the head Book soon

Likely causes

  • Moisture and dirt remain inside the head.
  • A drainage fault leaves standing water.

Pricing

What shapes the ductless estimate

City & Suburban offers upfront pricing with no hidden fees. Installation cost depends on the rooms, equipment combination, and routes through the building. Repair cost depends on the diagnosed fault and parts needed. Compare the complete scope, including drainage and access, rather than a price for one indoor head.

1 Number of zonesOne room and several closed bedrooms need different layouts. More heads add equipment, connections, drainage routes, and service access needs. A quote should identify the rooms served and the compatible indoor and outdoor combination, rather than count heads alone.
2 Room conditions and seasonal useAn attic with roof exposure differs from a shaded condo bedroom. Insulation, windows, air leakage, and winter use affect the equipment choice. A cooling-only comfort goal also differs from relying on the same system for heat. The quote should reflect the intended use.
3 Head placement and piping routeA convenient wall is not always a useful location for airflow or maintenance. The line set route, wall construction, exterior finish, and access all affect labor. Agree on where piping will be visible and how wall openings will be finished before comparing proposals.
4 Condensate drainageCooling creates water that needs a dependable route away from the indoor head. A short, accessible drain route differs from a route that needs additional drainage equipment. The proposal should explain where water goes and leave access for future cleaning or repairs.
5 Outdoor access and electrical workA ground-level location, a shared roof, and a narrow side passage present different access constraints. Electrical supply and equipment clearances also affect the scope. Condo association requirements can limit placement. Include these details before treating two installation estimates as equivalent.
6 Repair scope and compatibilityA filter problem differs from a leak, damaged fan, or control fault. On a multi-zone system, replacing one head may depend on compatibility with the outdoor unit. Model numbers, part availability, and the condition of connected equipment help determine whether a repair is practical.

Rooms without ductwork

Ductless layouts for Chicago homes

Single-room ductless mini-split

An addition or enclosed room can have a dedicated comfort zone without extending ducts. The head needs a place that lets air reach the occupied space. Outdoor placement, piping, and drainage still need to work together. Plan one indoor head and an outdoor location with clear airflow and service access.

Ductless for several rooms

A multi-zone layout can serve several rooms through a shared outdoor unit and compatible indoor heads. The number of heads does not settle capacity or mode limits. A proposal should identify the complete combination and the rooms served. Where the selected system uses a branch box, its location must remain accessible for service.

Ductless for an attic

Roof exposure, insulation, and sloped ceilings shape an attic layout. A sloped ceiling can limit head placement; leave room above the head and a safe way to reach its filters.

Ductless for an addition

An addition can have a dedicated comfort zone without depending on air traveling through a doorway. Separate control lets an addition respond to its own sun exposure and room use.

Ductless for a condo

Condo planning brings the indoor location together with association rules, shared exterior space, and service access. An attractive wall location cannot settle those outside constraints. Agree on approvals and routes before work begins. Association approval should precede a wall penetration or any work affecting common property.

Ductless in a two-flat

A two-flat may have different comfort needs on each floor. Zone planning should follow room use and doors. Ownership and responsibility for service also matter. Per-floor zoning should keep shared outdoor equipment accessible for service.

Ductless HVAC questions

Can a ductless mini-split serve an addition without new ducts?

A ductless mini-split can serve an addition without extending the existing ductwork. The room still needs a suitable indoor head location, an outdoor unit location, and a route for refrigerant lines and drainage. City & Suburban offers ductless installation and repairs all makes and models.

Does one indoor head cool several closed bedrooms?

A single-zone system pairs one head with one outdoor unit. One head cannot give several closed bedrooms separate control: walls and closed doors limit airflow. A multi-zone system uses compatible heads sharing an outdoor unit, but mode limits still depend on the model. A bedroom used with the door shut may need its own head.

Can a ductless system provide both heating and cooling?

A ductless system designed for heating and cooling can provide both from the same equipment. Winter suitability depends on the selected model and its heating output at cold outdoor temperatures. An attic or addition needs a winter comfort plan, including whether another heat source must remain available.

What should a condo owner settle before ductless installation?

Condo planning should settle association approval, outdoor equipment placement, wall penetrations, drainage, and access for future service. Shared walls and roof space may limit the route even when the room has a clear place for a head. Written approval should precede work that affects common property.

What can a homeowner check when a ductless remote does nothing?

Check the remote batteries, displayed mode, and timer settings against the operating manual. Note any light pattern on the head before changing settings. A visible display does not prove the indoor and outdoor equipment are communicating. City & Suburban offers same-day service when the schedule allows.

What information helps with booking a ductless repair?

Provide the indoor and outdoor model numbers, affected rooms, current mode, and any error display. Note whether all heads stopped together or only one room lost comfort. City & Suburban repairs all makes and models. Photos taken safely from floor level can help describe a leak or the location of the equipment.

Is there a maintenance plan for a home with ductless equipment?

City & Suburban offers maintenance plans with seasonal check-ups, priority dispatch, and member discounts. Before enrolling, confirm how the plan applies to the ductless equipment and how many heads are included. A home with several zones should identify each indoor head and the shared outdoor unit at booking.

Which ductless brands does City & Suburban install and service?

City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment and repairs all makes and models. An existing mini-split from another manufacturer can still be serviced. Provide the indoor and outdoor model numbers at booking so the service request identifies the equipment and connected heads.

What backs a ductless installation?

City & Suburban gives an upfront written price before work, with no hidden fees. Equipment warranty terms come from the manufacturer and should be confirmed in writing with the quote. The written terms should identify coverage, registration requirements, and any exclusions, including how labor and future service are handled.

Does a ductless system cost less to run?

Variable-speed ductless equipment can use less electricity than single-speed window units or resistance heat by adjusting output to the room load. Savings depend on the selected model, weather, insulation, settings, and the equipment replaced. Compare expected use for the actual rooms; lower running costs are not guaranteed.

Ductless room planning

Ductless Mini-Splits in Chicago: Zoning, Placement, Repair and Install Day

By the City & Suburban team · Updated October 2026 · 17 min read

In this guide

  1. What is a ductless mini-split, and how does it heat and cool without ducts?
  2. Which Chicago buildings end up with no ductwork, and where does a mini-split fit?
  3. Single-zone or multi-zone: how many ductless heads does a home need?
  4. Where do ductless heads, line sets and drains belong in an older building?
  5. How does a ductless system handle heat in a Chicago winter?
  6. What usually goes wrong with a ductless mini-split, and what fixes it?
  7. What maintenance does a ductless system need, and how long should it last?
  8. What happens on a ductless installation day, and what does the City require?
Book a ductless service visit Call (773) 238-3838

Ductless mini-splits answer a problem that is ordinary in Chicago: a room, a floor or a whole condo with no ductwork to carry conditioned air. A greystone attic. A coach house. A rear addition off a steam-heated two-flat. This guide covers how a mini-split works, which buildings suit one, how single-zone and multi-zone systems differ, where heads and line sets belong in masonry walls, what usually fails, what maintenance keeps a system honest, and what a correct installation day looks like. City & Suburban has worked on Chicago systems since 1952.

Key takeaways

  • A ductless mini-split moves heat through a copper refrigerant line instead of ducts, so one outdoor unit can cool a room in July and heat it in January.
  • Cook County Assessor records count 306,261 of 439,398 residential properties in the eight Chicago townships with no central cooling, which is why ductless work is common here.
  • Zone count matters more than head size: one oversized head in a hallway conditions the hallway, while a multi-zone system gives each room its own control.
  • Most ductless service calls trace back to airflow or water, not refrigerant: a fouled blower wheel, a blocked drain line or a dirty outdoor coil.
  • Installing new equipment generally needs a City of Chicago permit; whether other work needs one is worth confirming with the City.

What is a ductless mini-split, and how does it heat and cool without ducts?

SHORT ANSWER

A ductless mini-split is two pieces: an outdoor compressor unit and one or more indoor heads, joined by a copper refrigerant line set instead of ductwork. The system moves heat in either direction, so the same equipment cools in summer and heats in the colder months. City & Suburban installs and repairs ductless systems in Chicago homes where no ducts exist, or where adding them would mean losing ceiling height.

Picture a rehabbed attic in a Logan Square two-flat. The space gets steam heat from the building below and a window unit wedged into a dormer. In July the room runs eight degrees warmer than the floor beneath it. In March the heat arrives whether the room needs it or not. No duct reaches the third floor, and adding one would cut into the only closet. This is the room a mini-split was built for, and the one case where cooling services and heating arrive in the same cabinet.

The usual fix is a stack of appliances. A window unit for summer, a space heater for winter, a box fan to push air down the stairs. The cost lands in three places. The window is blocked from May to October, and the noise sits in the room. The electric bill climbs too, because resistance heat uses more electricity than a heat pump for the same warmth and a single-speed window unit cycles at full output. Some of these appliances have thermostats, but each serves only the spot where it sits.

What changed is the compressor. An inverter-driven compressor varies its speed instead of cycling on and off, so a mini-split can hold a room within a degree at part load. The line set, usually two insulated copper tubes and a control cable, replaces the duct entirely. A reversing valve sends heat the other way in winter, pulling warmth out of cold outdoor air. One cabinet outside, both seasons, controlled room by room.

A ductless quote starts as a room question before an equipment question. Which rooms are uncomfortable, what the walls are made of, where an outdoor unit can sit, how far the line set has to run. City & Suburban sends NATE-certified technicians, diagnoses before anything is quoted, and prices upfront with no hidden fees. Installed equipment is American Standard, and City & Suburban repairs all makes and models, so a mini-split left behind by another installer is still serviceable.

The scale of the problem sits in the public record. Cook County Assessor data for the eight townships covering Chicago counts 439,398 residential properties, and 306,261 of those have no central cooling. That count covers houses and small multi-family buildings, not large apartment buildings. Ductless is not a niche product in this city. For much of the housing stock it is the only route to cooling that does not start with new ductwork.

Parts of a ductless mini-split system and what each one does
PartWhere it sitsWhat it does
Outdoor unitGrade-level pad, flat roof or wall bracketCompressor and coil; moves heat into or out of the building
Indoor headHigh on a wall, or as a ceiling cassetteBlows conditioned air into one room and holds that room's setting
Line setThrough a sleeve in the wall, in a chase or under a coverTwo insulated copper tubes carrying refrigerant both ways
Control cableBundled with the line setLets the head and the outdoor unit talk and share a power feed
Condensate drainOff the back of the head, by gravity or a small pumpCarries water off the indoor coil to a drain or outside
Branch boxAttic, closet or beside the outdoor unit on multi-zone jobsSplits refrigerant among the heads the model supports
Wall control or remoteIn the room the head servesSets temperature, fan speed and mode for that zone alone

Pro tip: A mini-split head is a piece of furniture on the wall for the next fifteen years. Decide the location around the room's layout, not around the shortest path for the line set.

Which Chicago buildings end up with no ductwork, and where does a mini-split fit?

SHORT ANSWER

Much of Chicago's older housing stock heats with steam or hot water and may have no usable air ducts. Additions, attics and coach houses were finished long after the mechanical layout was set. City & Suburban installs ductless systems in exactly those spaces: third-floor conversions, garden units, sunrooms and rooms over a garage. Condos where a shaft wall blocks every duct route are the other common case.

Four building types come up again and again. The pre-1940 greystone or two-flat with steam and hot-water heat and often no usable duct in the building. The bungalow with a finished attic above a single trunk line. The condo carved out of a courtyard building, where the only wall facing outside is the one with the windows. And the rear addition, built decades later onto a house whose mechanical room is forty feet away.

The default answer is to extend the ducts. In a masonry building that means a soffit down a hallway, a chase cut through a closet, or joists drilled where drilling becomes a structural question. The homeowner pays twice: once for carpentry and patching that adds no comfort, and again in lost space. In a condo, the board has to approve the work before any of it starts.

A single-zone mini-split often needs only a small sleeve through one wall, sized to the manufacturer's line set and drain requirements. Multiple heads, fire-rated walls and condensate routes can need more penetrations or more work. Where the line set, control cable and drain share one hole, it is pitched down to shed water. This changes which rooms are candidates. A finished attic, a garden-level office or a four-season room can be conditioned without touching the rest of the building. The existing system is not asked to carry a load it was not sized for.

The building decides the system here, because the wall, the drain path and the outdoor location set the limits of what can be installed. Where ducts already exist and are in reasonable shape, an AC installation is the other route, and City & Suburban quotes that work too. City & Suburban is family-owned, has worked in Chicago since 1952, and serves 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs, so these building types are familiar ones.

Cook County Assessor records put 98,849 of those residential properties on hot water or steam heat, so many of these buildings may lack usable air distribution; an inspection confirms what is actually there. In West Chicago township, covering Wicker Park and West Town, 83.0% of properties date from before 1940. Ductwork was never part of the original plan across much of this city, and retrofitting it is a construction project rather than a mechanical one.

  • Finished attic or third-floor conversion, past the reach of the existing system
  • Coach house or room over a garage with no mechanical room of its own
  • Rear addition or four-season room built long after the original layout
  • Garden unit or basement office that runs cold in winter and damp in summer
  • Condo in a courtyard building heated by the building, with no chase for a duct
  • One room that has always been the hottest or the coldest in the house

Single-zone or multi-zone: how many ductless heads does a home need?

SHORT ANSWER

One head conditions one open space. It does not push air around a corner or up a stairwell. A single-zone system suits one room or a small open floor. A multi-zone system runs several heads off one outdoor unit, each with its own control; how many depends on the model, its minimum modulation and its shared-mode limits. City & Suburban prices ductless work upfront with no hidden fees, so the cost of a second or third zone is clear before the job starts.

The first request is almost always for one large head to handle a whole floor. In a 1920s Chicago layout with a center hallway and doors on both sides, that does not work. Conditioned air follows the shortest return path, so the hallway reaches the setting, the head satisfies and shuts down, and the two bedrooms stay as warm as before. Open-plan rehabs are the exception, not the rule.

The common response is to oversize. A head rated well above the room's load feels safer, and one zone is a cheaper quote than three. The cost arrives later. An oversized head reaches the setting fast, drops to its minimum output, and stops pulling humidity out of the air, so the room feels clammy at 72 degrees. Short cycling also wears the parts that cycle.

The mechanism most quotes skip is minimum capacity. A multi-zone outdoor unit has a floor below which it cannot modulate, and every head draws from that same compressor. Three small heads on a large outdoor unit can leave the system running above the load of any single room. Matching each head to its room, and the sum of the heads to the outdoor unit, is the real design work. The same modulation limits show up in any heat pump service call on a ducted system.

Zone layout is the decision that comes before equipment selection on this kind of job. A two-zone system with correctly matched heads usually holds temperature better than a three-zone system built around one oversized head. City & Suburban quotes ductless work with upfront pricing and no hidden fees, and financing through Wells Fargo Home Projects is available subject to credit approval.

Ductless work appears in City of Chicago permit records as heat pump activity. In the 24 months to August 2026, 150 permits mention heat pump work, about six a month, with a median declared value of $25,200 across whole projects. Twenty-seven were express equipment permits, median $18,096. The volume is small, which is part of why real experience with these systems is uneven across the trade.

Pro tip: Count the doors. Any room that closes off from the head's airflow needs its own zone, a transfer path, or a different plan.

Where do ductless heads, line sets and drains belong in an older building?

SHORT ANSWER

Head placement decides comfort, noise and how the installation looks for the next decade. A wall head wants clear throw across the room, a return path back to its underside, and several inches of clearance above it. Head location, sleeve position and drain route are settled before any hole is drilled, because moving a head later means patching brick. City & Suburban installs and repairs ductless systems across 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs.

Chicago walls complicate this. Exterior walls are often solid masonry three bricks thick, and interior walls may be plaster over lath. A 1920s layout rarely offers a chase from the third floor down to grade. Add a bay window, a fire escape and a lot line four feet away, and the number of workable routes drops fast. The best wall for comfort and the easiest wall to drill are seldom the same wall.

Many installs follow the easiest path for the crew. The head goes on the wall nearest the outdoor unit. The line set runs down the front of the building in a white cover, and the drain ties into whatever is close. The homeowner lives with the result. Air blows straight into a ceiling fan, a cover crosses the front facade, and a drain backs up into the head two summers later.

Three details decide whether that happens. Throw: a wall head should blow along the long axis of the room, not into a wall six feet away. Fall: a gravity drain needs roughly a quarter inch of drop per foot, or else a condensate pump with a safety switch. Length and lift: every line set has a maximum run and a maximum height difference, and both change the refrigerant charge the system needs.

Good practice on an older building is to agree head locations, sleeve position and drain fall before drilling. The line set then runs on the least visible elevation the building allows. Mounting hardware belongs in masonry rather than trim, and the sleeve is sealed and pitched so rain drains outward. City & Suburban works in 13 Chicago neighborhoods and 8 suburbs, listed on the service areas page.

Drain trouble is not theoretical in Chicago condos. Larry V. (Jul 2025) called about "water leaks related to a clogged condensation pipe above my condo unit". The outdoor equipment got a look on the same trip. Any indoor coil that makes water needs somewhere for that water to go, by gravity or by pump. A head mounted without that plan sends the water down the wall.

Pro tip: Before the hole is drilled, stand where the furniture goes and look at the wall. A head six inches off center is a fifteen-year annoyance.

How does a ductless system handle heat in a Chicago winter?

SHORT ANSWER

A ductless head heats by reversing the refrigerant cycle, and in one room it often becomes the main heat source for that space. Capacity falls as the outdoor temperature drops, and the system pauses to defrost its outdoor coil. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment. Whether the building's existing heat stays in place as backup depends on the model's cold-weather output, the room's heat loss and the building's requirements, so confirm the winter plan in the quote.

Chicago asks more of a heating system than a cooling one. A rehabbed attic that needs a window unit for ten weeks may need heat for six months. In a condo where the building supplies heat, the code baseline is a floor rather than a comfort setting. A top-floor room facing north often sits below it on a windy February night.

The usual plan treats ductless as a summer purchase and ignores the heating half. The head gets sized for the cooling load, which in Chicago is the smaller of the two loads. Then December arrives and the zone cannot hold temperature on a design-day morning. The electric space heater comes back out, which is the most expensive heat in the building.

Two mechanisms explain that. Output drops as the outdoor temperature falls, because there is less heat in the outdoor air to move. What usually goes wrong with a ductless mini-split, and what fixes it?

Most ductless service calls come down to airflow or water rather than refrigerant. Two complaints dominate ductless calls. A head that runs but no longer cools, and a head that drips down the wall in July. Both tend to show up in the third or fourth summer. Both get lived with for a few weeks first, because a mini-split failing slowly is easy to ignore.

The common assumption is low refrigerant. A sealed system does not consume refrigerant, so a system that is low has a leak, and adding more without finding the leak buys one season. The other default move is a filter rinse. Rinsing the two mesh filters takes five minutes and helps, but it does not reach the part that actually fouls.

contentFields.value: A mini-split is quiet, and that is the problem. A system that fouls slowly never announces it, so the first sign is a drip, or a summer where the room never gets below 76 degrees. Meanwhile the equipment sits in the room, pulling the room's dust through itself all season. Typical service life for this equipment is 15 to 20 years, and a neglected head rarely gets there.

contentFields.value: Most ductless systems in Chicago get no service at all. Nothing sits in a basement to walk past, and no filter rack reminds anyone. Multi-zone jobs run longer. Commissioning is the step that decides how the system performs in year four. City & Suburban installs American Standard equipment and quotes upfront with no hidden fees.

contentFields.label: P: Installation day in an occupied Chicago condo is a logistics problem as much as a mechanic
contentFields.value: Installation day in an occupied Chicago condo is a logistics problem as much as a mechanical one. Elevator reservations, a route for a ladder, a neighbor's parking space, and a lot line that leaves four feet for an outdoor unit. On a flat-roof building the equipment goes up the stairs. None of that changes the mechanical work, but it changes the schedule.

contentFields.value: The fast version of this job skips the part nobody sees. The line set gets connected, the valves opened, and the system started within the hour. Skipping the nitrogen pressure test and the vacuum leaves air and moisture inside a sealed system, and moisture plus refrigerant oil makes acid. That failure arrives in year four, long after the crew has gone.

contentFields.label: P: Commissioning is what separates one install from another. A nitrogen pressure test holds t
contentFields.value: Commissioning is what separates one install from another. A nitrogen pressure test holds the joints under pressure before any refrigerant enters. A deep vacuum pulls the system down to a few hundred microns and then holds, proving it is dry and tight. Flare joints get torqued to spec rather than guessed, because a flare is the most common leak point on a ductless system.
